messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forensic Analyst
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mele was 46 when her husband died without warning, and in the months since, time in her life had begun to divide sharply into before and after. She is a forensic analyst, a detail-oriented woman who had spent years working with evidence, chain of custody, and the disciplined routines of a lab. On the day her husband died, that professional steadiness offered her no protection. He had collapsed suddenly at home. She remembered the scene not as a continuous sequence but as a set of brutal stills that returned to her intact: his body on the kitchen floor, the angle of one arm against the cabinet, her own hand slipping as she tried to reach him, the phone in her grip as she called for help. What came back with those images was sound. Even now she could hear, in her head, the emergency dispatcher’s voice asking questions she could barely answer, her own voice sounding strange and thin, and the terrible absence of any reply from her husband as she called his name.

When Mele tried to speak about that day in early sessions, she did not tell it in a smooth narrative. She would get to one of those moments—the tile under her knees, the dispatcher saying, “Stay with me,” the silence after she shouted for him—and then stop abruptly, flooded and unable to continue. She described the memory as if it attacked in pictures. A few seconds would appear in her mind with unnerving clarity, and the emotion that came with them was so intense that she had to shut down the conversation, look away, or grip the sides of the chair until it passed. She was not remembering it as something over and finished. She was colliding with fragments she could hear and see all over again.

In the weeks after his death, she had gone back toward her routines briefly, trying to act as though structure might contain what had happened. But her work became one of the clearest places where the loss confronted her. In the forensic lab, the controlled quiet, ringing phones, clipped procedural language, and sudden requests for urgent review all echoed too closely the sounds and pressure of that day in her kitchen. Some mornings she would sit in her car outside the building rehearsing the effort it would take just to walk in, then text that she was unwell or turn around and drive home. Other days she made it to her desk but left tasks untouched, staring at screens she could not focus on. For someone whose identity had long rested on precision and stamina, avoiding work felt humiliating, but going in felt unbearable.

At home, the evenings stretched into something she dreaded. Sleep meant surrendering the last hours in which she could still busy herself and hold the memories at a distance, so she began staying up later and later, moving through the house after midnight with the television on low or her phone in her hand, waiting until exhaustion forced her to bed. She knew she was making herself ill, but the alternative was lying in the dark with those images ready to return. Eating also became something she restricted rather than attended to. She described having no appetite, but there was also a deliberate edge to it: meals felt wrong, mechanical, almost like an insult to the fact that her husband was gone. Coffee replaced breakfast, dinner was skipped, and her body thinned as her days narrowed.

What had shifted most starkly was the way she understood her life. Mele had come to feel that something fundamental had been broken beyond repair. She said plainly that her life had been destroyed by what happened, not in a dramatic sense but as a statement of fact as she experienced it. The future she had assumed was there—shared routines, shared aging, ordinary plans—had vanished, and nothing she did now seemed connected to a life that still held shape or purpose. She no longer trusted the promises people made about safety, fairness, or the idea that life had any dependable order. If a person could be alive in the kitchen one moment and gone the next, then talk of meaning or protection seemed hollow to her. She spoke about having lost faith not only in other people’s reassurances but in life itself.

Her marriage had been central to the way she organized her world, and its sudden end left her moving through her own home as though it were the scene of something unanswerable. Over months, friends and colleagues saw less of her. At work her absences became noticeable; at home she withdrew into long wakeful nights and sparse, joyless days. By the time she sought help, the strain was visible in her appearance and in the effort it took her to tell even part of the story. What finally brought her in was the realization that she was no longer only grieving her husband; she was disappearing from her own life as well. She said she was frightened that if she kept going this way, there would soon be nothing left of the person she had been. At the same time, what she most hoped for was modest and painfully clear: not to forget him, not to erase what happened, but to be able to go to work, sleep at night, and live in a world that did not feel permanently emptied of meaning.
